abstract:
To investigate the role of N6-methyladenosine (m6A) RNA epigenetic modification in the development of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) resulting from high-voltage electrical burns (HVEB).
We established an HVEB-induced PTSD-like rat model, evaluating PTSD-like behaviors through a series of behavioral tests. m6A-sequencing (m6A-seq) and transcriptome sequencing (RNA-seq) were conducted to compare the differential profiles of hippocampal tissues between HVEB-PTSD rats and Sham controls. Bioinformatics analysis and Lasso regression were utilized to identify key candidate genes and relevant signaling pathways. Furthermore, we validated the expression levels of hub genes, m6A modification levels, and changes in downstream pathways using quantitative PCR (qPCR), immunofluorescence and Western blot techniques.
Behavioral evaluations indicated that HVEB significantly induced PTSD-like behaviors in the rats. Notably, the global m6A methylation levels in the hippocampal tissues of HVEB-PTSD rats were significantly elevated compared to those in the Sham group. The combined analysis of m6A-seq and RNA-seq, along with Lasso regression, pinpointed two candidate genes. Among these, Sostdc1 showed a strong negative correlation with FTO in both FPKM and qPCR analyses, with its m6A levels aligning with its mRNA expression. Conversely, Fgfbp3 was negatively correlated with FMR1 solely at the FPKM level, with its m6A modification and mRNA expression displaying opposite trends. Subsequent validation indicated that the protein expression of Sostdc1 was upregulated in the hippocampus of rats exhibiting PTSD-like symptoms, accompanied by alterations in the expression levels of crucial molecules within the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway. Finally, Golgi staining revealed that dendritic spine density in the hippocampal CA2/CA3 region was lower in the HVEB-PTSD group than in the Sham group.
Hippocampal m6A dysregulation and elevated Sostdc1 expression are molecular correlates of PTSD-like behavioral phenotypes following HVEB. The associated suppression of Wnt/β-catenin signaling supports the m6A-Sostdc1-Wnt axis as a candidate mechanism.
